sentences.text: Cricosaurus was an extinct marine reptile that lived in the ocean during the Late Jurassic period.
This animal was relatively small, with all known species measuring three meters or less in total body length.
Its body was streamlined with a finned tail, making it a more efficient swimmer than modern crocodiles.
Both juveniles and adults of C. araucanensis possessed well-developed salt glands, allowing them to drink salt water and eat prey with high ionic concentration without dehydrating.
The pelvis of Cricosaurus araucanensis features characteristics that create an unusually large pelvic opening.
The genus Cricosaurus was established by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1858 based on three skulls found in the Late Jurassic of Germany.
Wagner originally described a specimen in 1852 as 'Stenosaurus elegans' before reclassifying it as Cricosaurus in 1858 based on fossils from a quarry in Daiting, Bavaria.
The long-snouted species C. suevicus likely fed mostly on fish.
In its ecosystem, Dakosaurus maximus was the top predator while C. suevicus fed on fish.
Researchers suggest that viviparity, or live birth, was more likely than oviparity for Cricosaurus based on an evaluation of reproductive hypotheses.
Salt glands allowed Cricosaurus to drink seawater from birth and eat prey with the same ionic concentration as seawater, such as cephalopods, without dehydrating.
Cricosaurus belongs to the family Metriorhynchidae.
It is classified within the subfamily Metriorhynchinae.
The animal is part of the suborder Thalattosuchia.
Cricosaurus is part of the unranked order Mesoeucrocodylia.
It belongs to the parent group Rhacheosaurini.
Cricosaurus lived from the Oxfordian to the Valanginian stages, between 159 and 132.6 million years ago.
Fossils of Cricosaurus have been found in Late Jurassic deposits across England, France, Switzerland, Germany, Argentina, Cuba, and Mexico, as well as in the earliest Cretaceous of Argentina.
C. suevicus and Dakosaurus maximus lived contemporaneously in the Nusplingen Plattenkalk formation in southern Germany at the end of the Kimmeridgian stage.
It is debated whether Cricosaurus forms a monophyletic group, as some phylogenetic analyses have not supported its monophyly.
